summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own targeting transgender people. The framework a trans visitor to Punjab stands under is India's national law, and within Punjab the documented signal is institutional rather than criminal: Pride Amritsar cancelled the parade scheduled for 27 April 2025 at the Rose Garden after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition as the reason. The Washington Blade reported the cancellation on 23 April 2025. No state intervention to preserve the event is recorded in the audited sources, so organised religious opposition has compelled the disappearance of Punjab's annual public trans assembly.

The national statute governing transgender people in Punjab is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, receiving presidential assent on 5 December 2019 and in force since 10 January 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment recognising a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, the Act grants transgender people the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. Criticism of the Act holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Criminal-law protection weakened nationally in 2024. A five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India on 6 September 2018, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely; the replacement removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people. In Punjab specifically, no criminal exposure is recorded, but public trans visibility carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition that succeeded in stopping the 2025 Amritsar parade.
tangentialFactors:
Punjab's record differs from the country-level risk picture in one direction and matches it in another. The foreign assessment in the UK Home Office country note of December 2025 rates police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, which sits alongside the specific checkpoint incidents recorded at a Kolkata railway station, in Railway Protection Force custody in Assam in June 2024, at Chennai International Airport in November 2024 and at passport interview in February 2026. Country-level ratings therefore understate the friction a visibly trans traveller meets at screening points.

The Amritsar cancellation is an adjacent-turbulence indicator rather than a legal one. Opposition came from religious organisations, including a prominent faction and the faith's highest temporal authority, and the parade did not take place; the absence of recorded official support for the event suggests that public assembly risk in Punjab is driven by community pressure that authorities did not counteract.

The constitutional position of the recognition scheme remains unsettled. The Supreme Court issued notice on 27 January 2020 in a petition challenging the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and the March 2026 amendment narrowed the recognition route further, drawing the objection from activists that the change criminalises people who self-identify outside the historically accepted groups.
localsOnly:
Residents of Punjab are covered by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, establishes the National Council for Transgender Persons, and sets a penalty of six months to two years' imprisonment plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. The Act permits declaration of a self-perceived gender identity without sex reassignment surgery as recognised in the 2014 NALSA judgment, subject to the March 2026 amendment's limits on which identities qualify for legal recognition.

Domestic criticism of the Act centres on what it does not provide: it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. Residents also live under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the Indian Penal Code in July 2024 and dropped Section 377 along with the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences, a change trans communities say leaves them more exposed to assault.

Public assembly carries a documented local precedent. Pride Amritsar's 27 April 2025 Rose Garden parade was called off after resistance from Sikh religious organisations including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, which means the annual gathering did not occur and organisers attributed the decision to religious-group opposition.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Punjab-specific statute, ordinance or institution targeting transgender people appears in the audited sources for this jurisdiction; the finding that the Punjab signal is institutional rather than criminal rests on the absence of such material, and Punjab police conduct, hate-crime incidence and enforcement of the 2019 Act are not sourced here.

Procedures for changing gender markers on Punjab-issued identity documents, driving licences or ration cards are not sourced. Whether the March 2026 amendment's recognition limits have been applied by Punjab authorities, and whether the constitutional challenge noticed on 27 January 2020 has been decided, are unresolved in this inventory.

The Washington Blade report of 23 April 2025 is the sole source for the Pride Amritsar cancellation; whether the 2026 edition of the event proceeded, and whether any official body responded to the cancellation, are not sourced.
